issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette: Thomas sat in the corner of his agency’s intake office, tracing the worn edge of his desk while the memory of the assault remained locked behind his teeth. Two years prior, a man had dragged him into a narrow maintenance corridor behind the county counseling center, pinning him against concrete walls while a single flickering bulb cast long, suffocating shadows. Thomas knew exactly what had happened to him, yet whenever he tried to articulate it to his wife, his throat closed and the words dissolved into a thick, choking silence. When the recollection surfaced unbidden, a heavy wave of shame washed over him, immediately followed by the same visceral terror he had felt in that darkened hallway. That unnameable horror did not fade; it anchored itself to his nervous system, directly fueling his threat appraisal. He found himself scanning crowded clinic corridors, his eyes darting toward every shadow, convinced that footsteps behind him signaled the same predator returning. When he couldn’t locate anyone, his anxiety simply migrated to new vulnerabilities, steering him away from unfamiliar neighborhoods where he couldn’t map the exits or assess the sightlines. Whenever the shame and terror crept back in, Thomas’s mind immediately scrambled to control the intrusion. He tried to force the images out of his head, pressing his palms against his temples until his forehead ached, but the suppression only left his baseline arousal elevated. In the quiet hours, the unresolved rage crystallized into a relentless loop, keeping him awake as he replayed the event and fixated on how to make the man who hurt him pay. These mental efforts did not passively coexist with his symptoms; the very act of chasing revenge fantasies and pushing the trauma from his awareness actively pushed him toward avoidance. He stopped taking field visits, refusing to enter any small meeting room or conference space without propping the door wide open, convinced that confinement would strip him of control again. The hyper vigilance that had taken root quickly reshaped his daily routines. When things ran late—a delayed elevator, a traffic jam on the route to his familiar practice—his body assumed disaster was already unfolding, which drove him further into rigid avoidance and mental suppression. His refusal to enter enclosed spaces and his relentless scanning of parking lots only left his baseline arousal elevated, which in turn made his threat monitoring more aggressive. He caught himself checking every rearview mirror, pacing the perimeter of familiar buildings, and fixating on potential ambush points, each avoidance tactic feeding the very alarm system he was trying to quiet. The fear of being trapped became non-negotiable, and his steering clear of unfamiliar places only ensured that his nervous system never learned safety was possible outside his routine. That perpetually activated alertness did not remain one-way; it looped back into the trauma network. The constant checking behind him and the assumption that delays meant danger kept his nervous system in a state of high alert, which made the original memories surface more frequently and with greater intensity. Each time the shame and terror returned, his inability to find words for what happened left him feeling fractured, and the recurring threat appraisal kept him trapped in the same defensive posture. Over eighteen months, these habits calcified. Thomas, who once made house calls across three counties, now restricted himself to the agency’s main floor, telling his colleagues he was focusing on administrative work. His wife kept trying to draw him into shared outings, but he withdrew into rigid schedules and defensive explanations, terrified that surrendering control would leave him powerless again. What finally pushed him to the clinic was a panic attack during a site inspection when the fire alarm forced him into a cramped stairwell. He realized he was no longer helping others because he was too busy surviving his own past. He hoped therapy could untangle the shame from the terror, not so he could forget what happened, but so he could stop letting a decades-old violation dictate where he walked, who he trusted, and how he lived his days.
